clinicalPearls: Enteroviruses are Picornaviridae with single-stranded RNA and a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid; being non-enveloped they are acid-stable (survive the stomach), resist alcohol and detergent disinfectants, persist for days at room temperature, but are susceptible to chlorine-containing cleansers.

More than 50% of nonpolio enterovirus infections and over 90% of poliovirus infections are subclinical; when symptomatic, the most common picture is a nonspecific febrile illness ('summer grippe'), and in temperate climates disease clusters in summer and fall.

In children and young adults enteroviruses account for up to 90% of aseptic meningitis cases with an identifiable agent; CSF shows pleocytosis that shifts from neutrophil to lymphocyte predominance within a day, total cell count usually under 1000/uL, normal glucose, and normal-to-slightly-elevated protein.

A normal CSF glucose in enteroviral meningitis helps distinguish it from mumps meningitis, in which CSF glucose is low; enteroviral meningitis tends to be more severe in adults than children but neurologic sequelae are rare.

Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (most often coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71) is highly infectious with attack rates near 100% in young children; coxsackievirus A6 causes a more extensive atypical form, and a B16/EV71 epidemic in Taiwan (1998) and yearly EV71 epidemics in China since 2008 produced brainstem encephalitis, pulmonary edema/hemorrhage, and deaths, mostly in children 5 years or younger.

Herpangina (usually coxsackievirus A) produces grayish-white papulovesicular ulcerating lesions concentrated in the posterior mouth (soft palate, anterior tonsillar pillars, uvula) and, unlike herpetic stomatitis, is NOT associated with gingivitis.

Pleurodynia (Bornholm disease), usually coxsackievirus B, causes paroxysms of knifelike pleuritic chest or upper-abdominal pain lasting 15-30 minutes with tender muscles and possible pleural rub; WBC and chest x-ray are typically normal.

Enteroviruses cause up to one-third of acute myocarditis cases; patients (over two-thirds male, often neonates/adolescents/young adults) present after a respiratory prodrome with chest pain, arrhythmia, ST/T-wave changes and elevated cardiac enzymes; up to 10% progress to dilated cardiomyopathy.

Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (enterovirus 70, coxsackievirus A24) presents with sudden severe eye pain, subconjunctival hemorrhage, chemosis, and preauricular adenopathy; its abrupt onset and short course (recovery in ~10 days) distinguish it from adenoviral or chlamydial eye disease, and EV70 cases have been linked to paralysis during epidemics.

Humoral immunity is critical: patients with agamma-/hypogammaglobulinemia can develop chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis (often echovirus 11) with a dermatomyositis-like syndrome and chronic hepatitis, and may relapse even while on immunoglobulin; hypogammaglobulinemic patients can shed poliovirus for more than 20 years.

Human parechoviruses (HPeV, also Picornaviridae) mimic enteroviral disease (neonatal generalized disease, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, seizures, hepatitis, rash) but pan-enterovirus PCR does NOT detect HPeV, so a dedicated PCR is required; infant deaths have been associated with HPeV-1, HPeV-3, and HPeV-6.

Reoviruses are double-stranded RNA viruses; most childhood infection is asymptomatic or causes mild upper respiratory symptoms, and reovirus is only a rare cause of mild gastroenteritis or meningitis, with speculative (unproven) links of reovirus type 3 to neonatal hepatitis and biliary atresia.
harrison.pathophysiology: Enteroviruses multiply in the gastrointestinal tract. Based largely on poliovirus studies, after ingestion the virus infects mucosal epithelium and replicates in submucosal lymphoid tissue (tonsils, Peyer's patches), spreads to regional lymph nodes and into a viremic phase with replication in reticuloendothelial organs; a secondary viremia may seed other tissues and cause symptomatic disease. CNS entry is thought to occur via the bloodstream (viremia precedes neurologic disease), but evidence also supports direct neural spread: the poliovirus receptor is an immunoglobulin-superfamily member expressed at the neuromuscular end-plate, and animal/transgenic-mouse studies show that cutting the sciatic nerve prevents spinal-cord involvement after IM virus injection, implying axonal transport from muscle to anterior horn cells. Poliovirus is culturable from blood 3-5 days after infection (before neutralizing antibody); it is shed from the oropharynx up to ~3 weeks and from the GI tract up to ~12 weeks (over 20 years in hypogammaglobulinemia), and attenuated oral vaccine virus can revert toward neurovirulence during GI replication. Capsid protein VP1 is the main neutralizing-antibody target, conferring lifelong serotype-specific protection that does not prevent reinfection or shedding; IgM persists under ~6 months and IgG for life. Mucosal/secretory IgA limits GI replication and shedding, and breast-milk IgA is protective. Acute flaccid myelitis and poliomyelitis both target anterior horn cells of the spinal cord.
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial sepsis (especially in neonatal generalized enteroviral disease)
Partially treated bacterial meningitis (can be hard to exclude from enteroviral meningitis)
Mumps meningitis (distinguished by low CSF glucose, vs normal in enterovirus)
Rubella (enteroviral rubelliform rash lacks lymphadenopathy and occurs in summer)
Measles (enteroviral enanthems may mimic Koplik's spots)
Herpetic stomatitis (vs herpangina, which lacks gingivitis)
Adenoviral or Chlamydia trachomatis conjunctivitis (vs acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis)
infectionMimics: Adenovirus and Chlamydia trachomatis ocular infection
nonInfectiousMimics: Guillain-Barre syndrome (also associated with enterovirus but a key paralytic mimic)
Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (as a sequela/overlap of enteroviral myocarditis)
Erythema multiforme and other drug or immune exanthems
Type 1 diabetes mellitus (epidemiologically associated with prolonged enteroviral shedding)
Idiopathic dermatomyositis (chronic enteroviral infection in agammaglobulinemia mimics it)
additionalInvestigations: PCR is now the primary diagnostic method; pan-enterovirus reverse-transcription PCR detects all human enteroviruses (CSF PCR ~70-100% sensitive, over 80% specific, faster than culture) but does NOT detect parechoviruses.
CSF PCR is less likely positive if presentation is 3 or more days after meningitis onset or with EV71; in those cases throat or rectal swab PCR (less specific) should be considered.

Serum PCR is highly sensitive/specific for disseminated disease and useful for diagnosis/monitoring in immunodeficient patients on immunoglobulin whose cultures may be negative; antigen detection is less sensitive than PCR.

Viral culture of CSF, serum, body-cavity fluid, or tissue is positive less often but a positive result is diagnostic; throat isolation is more meaningful than stool because shedding is shorter; coxsackievirus A may need special cell lines or suckling-mouse inoculation.

For suspected poliomyelitis: obtain two or more fecal and throat swabs at least 1 day apart for culture; a positive stool culture within the first 2 weeks confirms diagnosis when CSF culture is negative, and any poliovirus isolate must be sent to CDC to distinguish wild-type from vaccine virus.

Serotype identification is mainly for epidemiology; serologic diagnosis (paired acute and ~4-week convalescent neutralizing titers, the most accurate method) is limited by the many serotypes and absence of a common antigen.
Dedicated parechovirus PCR (performed by CDC and research labs; often unavailable commercially) when HPeV is suspected.

In acute flaccid myelitis: spinal-cord MRI may show gray-matter changes; CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and mildly elevated protein; EV-D68 antibodies are most often found in CSF though the virus itself is rarely detected there.
redFlags: Neonatal enteroviral illness resembling sepsis with myocarditis/hypotension, fulminant hepatitis with DIC, meningoencephalitis, or pneumonia (serious disease most often in the first week of life, up to 3 months).
Rapid onset of flaccid limb paralysis after fever/respiratory symptoms (acute flaccid myelitis or paralytic enteroviral disease).
Brainstem encephalitis with myoclonus, tremor/ataxia, plus pulmonary edema or hemorrhage in young children (severe enterovirus 71 disease).
Bulbar involvement causing dysphagia, dysphonia, or respiratory insufficiency/circulatory collapse in poliomyelitis.
Chest pain, arrhythmia, ST-segment changes, and elevated cardiac enzymes after a respiratory prodrome (enteroviral myocarditis, risk of dilated cardiomyopathy).
Chronic meningoencephalitis or dermatomyositis-like syndrome in an agamma-/hypogammaglobulinemic patient.
harrison.prognosis: Most enterovirus infections are mild and self-limited, resolving within about a week. Enteroviral aseptic meningitis carries an excellent prognosis with rare neurologic sequelae (though CSF abnormalities can persist weeks); immunocompetent encephalitis patients generally do well. Pleurodynia resolves in days with rare recurrence; acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis usually recovers completely in ~10 days. Myocarditis in older children and adults usually resolves fully, but neonates often have severe disease and up to 10% progress to chronic dilated cardiomyopathy, with chronic constrictive pericarditis a possible sequela. In paralytic poliomyelitis most patients regain some function over weeks to months but about two-thirds have residual neurologic sequelae; postpolio syndrome has a generally good prognosis with slow progression and plateaus of 1-10 years. Acute flaccid myelitis usually leaves persistent neurologic deficits. EV71 CNS disease can leave lasting dysphagia, cranial-nerve palsies, hypoventilation, limb weakness/atrophy, and impaired cognition. HPeV infection is usually mild (HPeV-1) but has caused infant deaths.
pitfalls: Glucocorticoids are contraindicated in enterovirus infections.

A positive enterovirus culture from stool, nasopharynx, or throat does NOT prove disease causation, since these sites are colonized for weeks during subclinical infection; throat isolation is more meaningful than stool.
Pan-enterovirus PCR does not detect human parechoviruses, so HPeV can be missed unless a dedicated assay is used.
CSF PCR may be falsely negative if obtained 3 or more days into meningitis or in EV71 infection.
Neonatal enteroviral disease can be indistinguishable from bacterial sepsis; a recent viral illness in the mother is a useful clue.
Cultures may be falsely negative due to neutralizing antibody, unsuitable cell lines, or improper specimen handling.

Oral poliovirus vaccine can revert to neurovirulence (vaccine-associated/vaccine-derived poliomyelitis), with risk roughly 2000-fold higher in immunodeficient persons; tonsillectomy predisposes to bulbar polio and IM injections increase paralysis risk in the involved limb.
harrison.severityClassification: Poliovirus infection severity spectrum: asymptomatic (most) -> minor/abortive poliomyelitis (~5%: fever, malaise, sore throat, myalgia, headache, resolving in ~3 days) -> nonparalytic poliomyelitis/aseptic meningitis (~1%) -> paralytic poliomyelitis (least common; asymmetric, proximal-predominant weakness, may be bulbar/respiratory). Paralytic disease is more frequent in older individuals, pregnant women, and those exercising or experiencing trauma at symptom onset. Postpolio syndrome occurs 20-40 years after initial paralytic disease. Vaccine-associated paralytic risk is about 1 per 2.5 million OPV doses.
